column4: This ayah joins two roots named in the section: “judgment belongs only to God” (إن الحكم إلا لله), and God commands worship of Him alone, “that is the upright dīn” (ذلك الدين القيم). It directly links divine judgment, worship, and dīn as submission.
Jacob says that judgment belongs only to God (إن الحكم إلا لله) as he sends his sons toward Egypt and entrusts them to God; it brings the section's hakim language into the same family peril as 12:80.
The Prophet asks God, Creator of the heavens and earth, to judge between His servants concerning what they differed over; it is another direct plea for the final adjudication named in the section.
The ayah says the Lord will judge between people on the Day of Resurrection over what they differed about; this repeats the section's scene of disputes referred to God's judgment.

Noah pleads, “judge between me and them decisively” (فافتح بيني وبينهم فتحا) and save him and the believers; like 11:45, this is a distressed prophet entrusting an immediate conflict to God's judgment.

On that day sovereignty belongs to God, who judges between people; believers who did good are in gardens. The verse joins the section's mastery branch of d-y-n, final ḥukm, and the good outcome of 95:6.
This ayah exposes people who claim belief but seek judgment from ṭāghūt after being told to reject it; it is a specific opposing recourse to the call to God's judgment in 4:59.
After people divide, the ayah says God would judge between them on the Day of Resurrection over their disagreement; it is another direct formulation of the section's delayed judgment.
The command says, “as He originated you, so you will return” (كما بدأكم تعودون); this closely links the section's created human in 95:4 to the return in 95:5.
God begins creation and repeats it, then people return to Him to receive just recompense; this connects the section's creation, return, and dīn as requital.
God originates creation, repeats it, and to Him people return (ثم إليه ترجعون); this is a concise parallel to the section's movement from creation to return.
After describing the stages in the womb, the ayah says God forms the human being as another creation; it supplies a bodily account of the formation called taqwīm in the section.
The next ayah says that after this formation people will die; it continues the human sequence from 23:14 toward the section's return and final judgment.
The next ayah says people will be raised on the Day of Resurrection; it completes 23:14-15 with the return to judgment that follows the section's creation and fall.
The ayah explicitly says the Hour is coming and God will raise those in the graves; it makes the creation sequence in 22:5 bear directly on resurrection, the section's dīn-day question.
“This is the Day of Decision” (هذا يوم الفصل) is announced to those who denied it; the phrase gives another name to the judgment day glossed in the section as dīn.
The ayah calls the judgment day “the Day of Decision” (ليوم الفصل); it names the day by the separation and ruling that the section associates with dīn.
The next ayah repeats the question “what will make you know what the Day of Decision is?”; it intensifies the day-name in 77:13 before the surah describes it.
The ayah calls the appointed gathering “the Day of Decision” (يوم الفصل); it is a further direct formulation of dīn as the day of judgment.
“The Day of Decision has an appointed time” (إن يوم الفصل كان ميقاتا); this states the certainty and appointment of the judgment day that the section calls dīn.
The transgressors are described as not expecting an account (لا يرجون حسابا); this directly echoes the section's gloss of dīn as ḥisāb and its challenge to denial.
The ayah calls the day “the True Day” and says whoever wills may take a return to his Lord; it joins the section's final judgment and return motifs.
The deniers exclaim, “This is the Day of Judgment” (هذا يوم الدين) when it arrives; it is an exact formulation of the day they are asked not to deny in 95:7.
The ayah calls it the Day of Decision and says people are gathered with earlier peoples; it makes the judgment-day name in 77:13 concrete as a gathered court.
On that day true dominion belongs to the Most Merciful and it is hard for disbelievers; this develops the section's d-y-n branch of mastery and the boundary between outcomes.
Angels glorify their Lord while judgment is made among people with truth; it brings the section's link between the worshiped Allah and the final Judge into one scene.
The record is placed, people fear what it contains, and their Lord wrongs no one; this is a concrete accounting scene for the section's dīn as judgment and reckoning.
Abraham asks forgiveness for himself, his parents, and believers on “the day the account is established” (يوم يقوم الحساب); this is a prayer oriented toward the reckoning named in the section.
The promised reward is identified as “this is what you are promised for the Day of Account” (هذا ما توعدون ليوم الحساب); it states the requital side of the section's dīn gloss.
Moses seeks refuge in his Lord from every arrogant person who does not believe in the Day of Account; it gives the section's dīn-day judgment a concrete posture of fearing God's verdict.

God asks Abraham “Do you not believe?” and Abraham answers “Yes indeed” (قال بلى); in a discussion of reviving the dead, this is another exact instance of the negative-question answer pattern the section explains.

“Does man think he will be left neglected?” (أيحسب الإنسان أن يترك سدى) precedes the creation stages and resurrection question in the same surah; it makes explicit the section's implication that the human is not left without final judgment.
Every soul tastes death and receives its full recompense on the Day of Resurrection; the verse spells out the accounting and requital the section reads in dīn.
Every community is seen kneeling and called to its record; this gives the section's judgment-day image a collective scene and a bodily posture distinct from standing before the Lord.
God's word is true and sovereignty is His on the day the trumpet is blown; this joins the section's rule of the Judge to the appointed resurrection scene.

The ayah says that everything in heaven and earth belongs to God and that “the dīn is His continually” (وله الدين واصبا); here dīn is devoted submission, a distinct but relevant sense beside the section's Day of Judgment.

The ayah says “to God belongs the pure dīn” (ألا لله الدين الخالص) and contrasts this with worship through intermediaries; this connects the section's mastery/submission branch of d-y-n with its claim that Allah is the one worshiped and the Judge.
People are commanded to worship God sincerely, making the dīn purely His; this uses dīn as submission or worship, the secondary sense that helps explain the section's d-y-n and ilāh connection.

“For you is your dīn and for me mine” uses dīn for a way of worship, not the Day of Judgment meant in 95:7; that difference matters because the section also develops d-y-n as subjection and links Allah to worship.

The verse says Joseph could not have taken his brother under the king's dīn (في دين الملك), meaning the king's law or rule; this is a distinct legal sense of the root beside the section's dīn as divine judgment and reckoning.
All in the heavens and earth submit to God willingly or unwillingly and return to Him; this makes the section's d-y-n branch of subjection and its return-to-the-Judge motif explicit.

The prayer names God “Master of sovereignty” and asks Him to give or take dominion, honor or abase whom He wills; this supplies a concrete instance of the ownership and subjection in the section's d-y-n gloss.

This resurrection argument traces human formation through the womb, maturity, and possible return to decrepit age before affirming that God raises the dead; it offers a specific bodily counterpart to the section's movement from best formation toward a low state, though the two passages need not mean the same stage.

Human beings move from weakness to strength and back to weakness and old age; as a human-life sequence, it is a specific reversal beside 95:4-5's best formation and descent, though the section does not identify its “lowest” with old age.

The messenger is said to remove burdens and shackles from people; this reverses the section's bridle as a restraining instrument and distinguishes correction that holds back wrongdoing from restraints that are themselves lifted.

The section's dictionary image is a ring around a horse's jaw that restrains it; this ayah mentions tethered warhorses (رباط الخيل). This is a weak scene parallel because the verse is about military readiness, not a corrective bridle.
